15.bp: When you scan a real object or generate a 3D shape with AI, you get a jumbled tangle of polygons that's hard for artists to edit. To make the shape flexible for modeling—stretching, sculpting, changing how it bends—you need it organized into rows and columns of four-sided blocks, like a quilt. This is the invisible scaffolding that holds a digital shape together so humans can shape it without fighting chaos.
15.wh: Making that quilt automatically is exceptionally tricky. Most algorithms grind away and produce ugly, knotted layouts—spirals and dead ends and twisted bands—that force an artist to spend days cleaning up by hand. The computer can't easily 'think' about what makes a layout simple because topology (the connections between pieces) is a discrete puzzle with no smooth gradient to follow.
15.ap: This paper introduces a generation model trained to dream up simple quilt layouts directly. Instead of working with the tangled mesh itself, they convert it into something smoother: Chart Distance Fields, which measure distance across the surface in a continuous way. They feed noisy versions of this field into a diffusion model—like reversing a blurring process—and it learns to denoise toward plausible, neat layouts. They also built a big dataset by mining existing 3D repositories and recovering the quilt structure from good examples.
15.ww: By working in this continuous distance-field space, the model sidesteps the discrete nightmare. It can learn gradual transitions between messy and neat layouts, and diffusion naturally captures the varied patterns that make a layout simple (long straight lines, few branches). Training on real successful quilts means the model learns human taste, not arbitrary rules.
15.po: The system reliably generates layouts that are simple and artist-friendly, cutting tedious manual cleanup. Real test cases show it outperforms traditional algorithms and works on diverse shapes—from scanned objects to AI-generated characters—with robust, buildable results.

16.bp: Virtual cameras now capture real people and objects in 3D video—every moment, every angle. Storing and streaming this mountain of volumetric data is expensive; you need compression that's fast enough to use live and compact enough for transmission. This is the video codec for 3D.
16.wh: Existing compression methods either treat each frame in isolation (wasteful, ignoring that the shape barely changes frame-to-frame) or require expensive registration algorithms that track how surfaces move in time. Neither works well for real-time capture or large virtual worlds.
16.ap: The authors adapt vintage video-compression tricks from the 1980s and 90s—things like Discrete Cosine Transform (the math that powers JPEG) and motion compensation (predicting where a region moved based on nearby motion)—to compress volumetric 3D content frame by frame. They work with Truncated Signed Distance Fields, a standard way to represent captured surfaces, which is nice because it fits naturally into existing capture pipelines and doesn't need to track vertex-by-vertex motion.
16.ww: Video compression works because adjacent frames are nearly identical, and motion compensation exploits that: if you know a block shifted left, you can predict the next frame by copying and shifting. The same logic applies to 3D volumes shifting in time. Discrete Cosine Transform is mathematically efficient and hardware-friendly. No expensive learning or registration needed.
16.po: The codec runs in real-time at 30 FPS and cuts bitrate by roughly 35% compared to per-frame storage. On synthetic scenes with big motion, it reaches 12× compression—dramatically cheaper to store and stream live captured performance.

17.bp: You want a computer to generate signals draped over a wiggly surface (a curved mesh of triangles) the way a scattering pattern sits on a canvas or waves flow over landscape. But there's a catch: the training should work on one triangulated surface and automatically apply to any mesh, even if it's divided into triangles a different way.
17.wh: Meshes are arbitrary—the same shape can be split into triangles in a million different ways. Training a model on one particular triangle layout breaks immediately when you feed it a different triangulation of the same shape. Most generative models assume a fixed grid (like pixels in an image), so this problem doesn't exist for them.
17.ap: The paper adapts flow matching—a generative technique that reverses a blurring process—to work on meshes in a triangulation-agnostic way. The key innovation is choosing the right noise distribution: they use Matern noise, a mathematical construct from random fields theory, because its spectrum (its mathematical fingerprint) is invariant to triangulation. The denoiser learns to refine noisy mesh signals using PoissonNet, a method that works in the gradient domain and doesn't care about triangle layout.
17.ww: The spectrum of a noise distribution captures its essential character independent of how you sample or discretize it. Matern noise has this universal property built in. By working in gradient space, the model thinks about local slopes, not absolute positions—another triangulation-agnostic quantity. This lets the model learn the intrinsic geometry of the surface, not artifacts of the mesh.
17.po: The system generates realistic elastic poses and humanoid positions on meshes with over a million triangles, and seamlessly generalizes to any triangulation of the same shape—no retraining needed. It beats prior methods in both quality and generality.

18.bp: Engineering and science often need volumetric meshes made of tetrahedra—chunks filling a 3D shape—to run simulations (stress, heat, flow) or prepare models for 3D printing. Making these high-quality meshes is a bottleneck: traditional algorithms fail on realistic shapes with tight corners and ugly angles.
18.wh: Sharp corners in the input (acute angles) wreck Delaunay refinement, the standard algorithm for tetrahedral meshing. When the input has a corner, the algorithm struggles to terminate gracefully and produces badly-shaped tetrahedra. Current tools like Tetgen fail on a third of real models.
18.ap: The authors modify the input shape by chamfering: they slice off the sharp corners with small bevels, creating rounded transitions. On this smoothed input, Delaunay refinement produces clean tetrahedra. Then they reinsert the removed corner material, accepting a small number of distorted tetrahedra localized to those regions. They use modern mathematical tricks—clever indirect predicates and implicit point representations—to guarantee numerical robustness through all stages.
18.ww: Chamfering removes the root cause of failure (acute angles). Delaunay refinement is mathematically elegant and guaranteed to terminate on smooth inputs. Reinserting the corners separately means imperfection is localized and predictable. Using indirect geometric predicates means the algorithm never computes exact coordinates, avoiding floating-point catastrophe.
18.po: The system succeeds on all 3942 models in a standard benchmark, whereas the best prior tool failed on 37% of them. Mesh quality matches the best existing methods, with robust handling of diverse, difficult real-world shapes.

19.bp: A robot tidying a messy home needs to understand what objects belong where—not just by rote rule, but by reasoning about what each surface is for, what you might put on it, and what you prefer. This combines common sense, physical understanding, and personal taste into a task-planning problem.
19.wh: Traditional approaches either rely on hand-coded rules (fragile and not personal) or ignore context entirely. A bowl can go on a table, but maybe not your living-room coffee table. The space between true understanding (semantic, preferential) and brittle automation is vast.
19.ap: The authors use a scene graph—a structured representation of objects and their spatial relationships—as the starting point. They feed this graph to a large language model to enrich it: each surface object (table, shelf, counter) is augmented with affordances—learned descriptions of what can be placed on it, conditioned on context. New abstract relationships are discovered and added to the graph. Then the robot plans by finding misplaced objects and determining the best receptacle for each, guided by the enriched graph.
19.ww: Large language models encode world knowledge—what kitchens look like, what typically holds what—learned from text. The scene graph makes this knowledge concrete and spatial: the model can reason about "this shelf in this room" rather than abstractions. By aligning affordances with user preference (learned from context), the system balances common sense with individual choice.
19.po: The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on detecting misplaced objects and choosing proper homes for them, in both simulated and real robotic systems. It generalizes to unseen home layouts without retraining, and improves as it observes user corrections.

20.bp: Digital painting brushes in software like Photoshop blend colors and mix textures. Currently most do this with heavy computation or look mushy. You want a brush that realistically simulates fluid flow—the way a bristle pushes and swirls paint—while staying sharp and running fast on the GPU.
20.wh: Real physics simulation of fluid flow is expensive and grid-based—it bloats memory and destroys fine detail. Simpler approaches fake it, but lose the tactile realism of bristles moving through paint. The tension is between physical fidelity and speed.
20.ap: The authors design brushes based on potential flow theory—the mathematics of fluid moving around a cylinder. They derive a fast, continuous velocity field for a brush tine, then use GPU-friendly tricks to track how particles drift through this field. Instead of simulating from scratch each stroke, they precompute displacement fields (Reverse-Drift Functions) that encode what happens when you insert, drag, and lift the brush. These stack together like layers, so complex brush paths compose from simple building blocks without needing to resimulate.
20.ww: Potential flow gives an analytical (closed-form) solution instead of requiring numerical solving. Drift functions let you compose effects: a complex stroke is just a chain of simpler operations, each captured as a displacement map. Working in image space and composing in shaders means every pixel is independent—parallelizes perfectly on modern GPUs.
20.po: The system renders realistic, sharp mixing effects in real-time at arbitrary resolution, with no grid-induced blur and zero numerical drift over time. Painters can produce complex, natural-looking results with minimal latency, and it integrates into production tools like Houdini.

21.bp: Real objects—a sandwich, a layered rock, a foam material—are made of multiple materials or phases nested inside each other, with boundaries between them. You want a compact, elegant representation that lets you model all of this at once, render it fast, and do physics-based operations on it like ray tracing.
21.wh: Most methods for representing shapes inside computers use signed distance fields (a function that tells you how far you are from the surface). They work beautifully for single materials, but extending them to multiple materials, interfaces, and complex topology is clunky and expensive.
21.ap: The authors introduce the PhaseTree, a hierarchical tree of primitives (spheres, boxes, bent shapes) combined with composition and warping operators, that directly represents a multiphase object. Each phase has its own signed distance, and the tree structure lets you build complex arrangements by combining simpler pieces. It's like a Lego instruction manual: layers of assembly that build up to the whole.
21.ww: The tree structure mirrors how you'd think about building the object: start with phases, layer them, warp them to fit. Signed distance is preserved through composition (the union of two signed-distance objects is still a valid signed distance). This means classical algorithms designed for single-phase shapes—like ray marching—extend almost automatically to multiphase objects. The hierarchy keeps memory tight and computation smooth.
21.po: The system runs ray tracing (a key rendering algorithm) with only 25% slowdown compared to single-phase, yet handles complex topologies and material boundaries seamlessly. It integrates into existing graphics pipelines without modification, and users can treat single and multiphase workflows identically.

22.bp: In hand-drawn 2D animation, filling in the frames between key poses (inbetweening) is tedious. When one character stands in front of another, strokes get hidden behind the foreground figure. Animators manually redraw hidden strokes, hide them, and manage layers frame by frame—laborious busywork.
22.wh: Occlusion breaks automated inbetweening: if you don't explicitly draw a hidden stroke in both keyframes, interpolation fails. Standard approaches either ignore hidden strokes or require manual intervention for each one.
22.ap: This paper introduces LayerInbetween, which predicts occlusion and handles it automatically. It learns to infer which strokes are hidden and at what layer depth, then uses a module called Global-Local Layer Transformation to guide how hidden strokes move and deform across keyframes. The system was trained on 17,000+ synthetic pairs of keyframes with known occlusions. During inbetweening, layers are resolved automatically so hidden strokes stay hidden without animator effort.
22.ww: By treating the layer structure as an intermediate variable the model learns, it gains a powerful constraint on stroke motion: strokes at the same layer move coherently, and layers don't penetrate each other. This layer-aware guidance is stronger than raw pixel matching. Machine learning on synthetic data lets the system generalize to hand-drawn styles it's never seen.
22.po: The system reliably inbetweens strokes even with occlusion, generalizing to diverse drawing styles and enabling more flexible editing of 2D animation. It removes a significant category of manual work, letting animators focus on creativity rather than frame-by-frame busywork.

23.bp: Creating 3D animated characters used to require three separate expert tasks: building a skeleton (rigging), painting how skin deforms around bones (skinning), and choreographing motion. AI now generates gorgeous static character models by the thousands—but they're frozen. Getting them to move requires the same tedious pipeline, one character at a time.
23.wh: Rigging and animation are currently independent: you rig a character, then animate it. But there's an implicit coupling—a character's skeleton should match its shape and move in ways consistent with its structure. Sequential pipelines ignore this coupling.
23.ap: ACT reformulates the problem: it treats rigging and animation as two views of the same thing. It uses a Vision Language Model to extract semantic clues from the shape ("this is an arm, this is a leg"), then conditions a Diffusion Transformer to jointly generate skeleton topology and motion as a unified sequence. A geometry-aware decoder ensures the skin deforms correctly around the generated skeleton. The same model does zero-shot rigging, text-guided animation, and motion completion by masking different parts of the sequence.
23.ww: Unifying rigging and animation in a shared latent space lets both inform each other: the skeleton respects the shape's structure, and motion respects the skeleton's degrees of freedom. Treating static pose and motion as a sequence in time is natural—the model learns that skeletal configuration and motion are linked. A single end-to-end model eliminates brittle handoff points between pipeline stages.
23.po: The system rigs and animates non-humanoid characters in zero-shot mode (no retraining), generalizing robustly to diverse shapes. It replaces a multi-stage manual workflow with a single end-to-end model, dramatically accelerating character creation from generated assets.

24.bp: Imagine standing face-to-face with a holographic version of a friend, indistinguishable from real. This requires capturing their motion, inferring how light bounces off their clothes and skin, and predicting how they'd look under different lighting—all from a head-mounted camera looking outward. This is the foundation for true mixed-reality presence.
24.wh: Existing methods solve pieces separately: capture without relighting, or require studio environments. Capturing everything simultaneously from a single viewpoint (the HMD camera) while inferring appearance under novel lighting is vastly harder than studio capture.
24.ap: EgoRelight combines three components: stereo cameras on the head-mounted display capture dense depth maps, which drive an avatar mesh precisely. A neural appearance model learns to separate light-dependent shine (specularity) from permanent color (diffuse), using a specialized ray-sampling strategy that generalizes to unseen lighting without relying on rigid mathematical models of material. Finally, the system estimates the surrounding light environment as a high-dynamic-range map, so the avatar can be relit in any scene.
24.ww: Depth maps give geometric ground truth, reducing ambiguity in appearance inference. Separating specular (view-dependent) from diffuse (view-independent) components makes the appearance model simpler and more transferable to new lighting. Ray-sampling strategy lets the model focus on regions that matter most perceptually, improving generalization beyond training lighting.
24.po: The system produces photorealistic, relightable avatars from egocentric video alone—no studio needed—and renders them seamlessly in any lighting environment. This unlocks practical mixed-reality telepresence with convincing appearance.

25.bp: Mountains are carved by water and gravity over millions of years. Landscapes erode, valleys deepen, sediment settles downhill—these processes are fundamental to terrain formation. Computer graphics wants to simulate this and create believable, complex landscapes automatically, with deltas and braided rivers.
25.wh: Water flow and sediment transport happen over vastly different timescales. Water responds in minutes; bedrock erosion takes millennia. Simulating both together is computationally nightmarish. Prior methods made simplifying assumptions (like Stream Power Law) that miss important behaviors.
25.ap: The authors develop a particle-based stochastic method that relaxes those simplifying assumptions. Individual particles represent water or sediment parcels that move, collide, and interact according to momentum conservation—more general physics. The method parallelizes beautifully and tolerates the varied timescales by using statistical averaging rather than synchronized updates.
25.ww: Particle methods are inherently parallel: each particle's motion is independent until collision. Stochasticity handles timescale mismatch: millions of tiny movements sum to larger geomorphological changes without explicit timestep coupling. Grounding in momentum conservation (rather than ad-hoc rules) means the model naturally captures multiscale phenomena.
25.po: The system produces realistic terrain with coherent basins, braided rivers, meanders, and deltas—complex geomorphological features that emerge from simple physics. It runs fast enough for interactive design and avoids artifacts plaguing prior methods.

26.bp: Real-time ray tracing (the gold standard for photorealistic images) is expensive. Current methods downsample the image (render at lower resolution, then enlarge) to save cost. But this treats every pixel equally—some regions are visually important, others are just background blur. You want to spend samples where they matter most.
26.wh: Traditional adaptive sampling is mathematically brittle at very low sampling budgets (below one sample per pixel), and deciding where to sample is a discrete choice that breaks gradient-based optimization. Balancing perceptual importance (foreground matters more than background) with sampling cost is hard.
26.ap: The authors develop an end-to-end neural system that learns to place samples adaptively. They use stochastic relaxation to convert discrete sampling decisions into differentiable operations, enabling stable training even at ultra-low budgets. Crucially, they train with a tone-mapping-aware loss that includes realistic image viewing (with gamma correction), preventing over-sampling of imperceptible regions. A pyramidal denoising filter recovers detail from sparse samples.
26.ww: Stochastic formulation of sampling placement allows gradient flow despite discrete choices. Tone-mapping-aware loss aligns optimization with human perception—a region that's perceptually identical after denoising doesn't need extra samples, even if it's technically noisier. Pyramidal denoising exploits multiscale structure in noise and detail.
26.po: The system produces high-quality, perceptually accurate images at sub-one-sample-per-pixel budgets, cutting rendering cost substantially. It learns to focus samples on regions that matter to the viewer, outperforming uniform superresolution approaches.

27.bp: Hair is stunning but geometrically complicated—thousands of strands, each curling and flowing. Creating realistic hairstyles by hand is expert work. You want a generative model that understands hair as a structured, semantic object (scalp regions, style layers) and can synthesize plausible variations, edit parts, and even imagine rare or fantastical styles.
27.wh: Most generative models treat hair as texture or a continuous field, mixing global structure (which strands go where) with local texture (curl and shine). This obscures semantic organization and makes editing and control nearly impossible. You end up with pretty blur, not controllable hair.
27.ap: HairGPT reformulates hair synthesis as a sequence problem: strands are generative primitives, and you build hair hierarchically, scalp region by region, from global layout to fine-grained style. It tokenizes geometry (converting 3D strand curves into discrete tokens) and uses spatial and structural decomposition—treating each scalp region separately, then building each strand from coarse (where it goes) to fine (its exact shape). This mirrors how digital artists actually groom hair.
27.ww: Sequence generation naturally captures hierarchy: earlier tokens set direction, later tokens refine. Spatial and structural decomposition reduces complexity: each subproblem is simpler and more learnable. Aligning the model with artist workflow means semantics (scalp region, strand layer) emerge naturally from the learning process.
27.po: The system generates complex, realistic hairstyles with fine detail, supports semantic editing of scalp regions and layers, and generalizes to rare styles and stylized domains. It transforms hair from opaque texture synthesis into a structured, controllable creative tool.

28.bp: Capturing 3D poses of multiple people from several camera angles is useful for VFX, sports, dance. A computer has to detect where people are in each 2D image, then figure out which 2D arms and legs correspond to the same person and reconstruct their 3D skeleton.
28.wh: Current methods treat all people's poses as a global optimization puzzle—a massive tangle of possible combinations. This makes the problem explosively complex and prone to mistakes. Additionally, they're locked to a specific 2D pose detector (OpenPose), preventing the use of newer, better detectors.
28.ap: TwinPose introduces twin poses: for each person detected in 2D, create a corresponding 3D pose that inherits the 2D detector's confidence and instance information. The twins aggregate 2D joints from other camera views that are geometrically consistent with that 3D pose. All twins live in a shared 3D space, but optimization happens person-by-person in learned person-specific subspaces, not globally.
28.ww: Optimizing within person-specific subspaces dramatically reduces complexity—N small problems instead of one giant tangle. Inheriting instance representation from the 2D detector lets newer detectors plug in seamlessly. Geometric consistency (rays from different cameras must intersect) is a powerful constraint that doesn't require global knowledge.
28.po: The system works with diverse 2D pose detectors, scales to many people without explosion in complexity, and leverages richer per-instance information from modern detectors. It achieves robust, efficient multi-person 3D pose reconstruction.

29.bp: Cloth, skin, water, and other soft materials deform dramatically. When you animate them, texture maps stretch and squash with the surface, resulting in ugly distortion. In nature, deforming materials rupture, wrinkle, compress, and expose internal layers—phenomena that change appearance in realistic ways. You want simulation that captures this.
29.wh: Simply following texture maps to deforming surfaces creates obvious artifacts: extreme stretching, baking distortion into the image. Physics-based texturing is expensive if you require actual simulation. The gap between per-pixel texture fixes and true physical behavior is wide.
29.ap: The authors propose wave-based procedural texturing driven by surface deformation. The algorithm uses standard deformation measurements (strain, curvature) to modulate texture procedurally in real-time on the GPU, mimicking physical phenomena like wrinkling and rupturing without simulating them. Multiple procedural algorithms capture self-similar details at different scales and advect pattern the way fluids do—all computed on the fly from the UV map and deformation, with no history or state needed.
29.ww: Procedural texturing is inherently parallelizable (each pixel computed independently) and stateless (only depends on current input). Grounding texture modulation in physical principles (strain causes wrinkling, rupture follows high-stress regions) makes results look natural and perceptually believable. Wave-based patterns capture self-similarity efficiently.
29.po: The system handles extreme deformations in real-time, producing convincing texture variation without physics simulation or memory overhead. It works with arbitrary deformation patterns, from severe crumpling to fluid-like flow, enabling rich animation of soft materials.
